chapter_summary:
Welcome to the world of Ethereum, the pioneering blockchain platform that truly unleashed the potential of smart contracts and decentralized applications (DApps). While Bitcoin introduced the concept of a decentralized digital currency, Ethereum expanded this vision to a decentralized global computer, capable of executing arbitrary code in a trustless environment. Understanding Ethereum is fundamental for any Certified Blockchain Professional, as many other platforms draw inspiration from its design or aim to solve its challenges.

At its core, Ethereum operates on a transaction-based state machine. Every transaction processed on the network transitions the global state of the blockchain from one valid state to the next. This state includes all account balances, contract code, and contract storage. Unlike Bitcoin, which primarily tracks unspent transaction outputs (UTXOs), Ethereum uses an account-based model. There are two primary types of accounts: Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) and Contract Accounts. EOAs are controlled by private keys and are used by humans or bots to send transactions, hold Ether, and interact with smart contracts. Contract Accounts, on the other hand, are controlled by their associated smart contract code. They have an address, hold Ether, and store data, but they can only be activated when an EOA or another contract sends a transaction to them, triggering their code execution. This distinction is crucial: EOAs initiate actions, while Contract Accounts react to them.

One of the most critical concepts in Ethereum is "Gas." Think of Gas as the fuel required to perform any operation on the Ethereum network. Every computation, every storage operation, every line of code executed by a smart contract consumes a certain amount of Gas. This mechanism serves several vital purposes. Firstly, it prevents infinite loops and denial-of-service attacks by ensuring that every operation has a cost. If a contract were to enter an infinite loop, it would eventually run out of Gas, and the transaction would revert, preventing network congestion. Secondly, Gas incentivizes miners (or validators, in the case of Proof-of-Stake Ethereum) to include transactions in blocks, as they receive the Gas fees. The Gas price, denominated in Gwei (a small unit of Ether), is determined by supply and demand for network resources. Users specify a "Gas limit" (the maximum amount of Gas they are willing to spend) and a "Gas price" (how much Ether they are willing to pay per unit of Gas). The total transaction fee is `Gas Used * Gas Price`. If a transaction runs out of Gas before completion, it reverts, but the Gas consumed up to that point is still paid to the miner – a common mistake for beginners to overlook.

The heart of Ethereum's computational power lies in the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). The EVM is a stack-based virtual machine that executes smart contract bytecode. When a developer writes a smart contract in a high-level language like Solidity, it is compiled into EVM bytecode. This bytecode is then deployed to the Ethereum blockchain as a Contract Account. When an EOA sends a transaction to this contract, the EVM on every node in the network executes the bytecode, ensuring that all nodes arrive at the same deterministic outcome. The EVM is an isolated environment, meaning that smart contracts cannot directly access network resources, file systems, or other external services. This isolation is a security feature, preventing malicious contracts from impacting the underlying operating system of nodes. However, it also means that contracts need external mechanisms (like oracles) to interact with the outside world. Understanding the EVM's stack-based architecture, memory, storage, and call stack helps in debugging and optimizing smart contracts. For instance, storing data in a contract's persistent storage (state variables) is significantly more expensive in terms of Gas than using transient memory during function execution, a key consideration for contract design and cost efficiency.

Common mistakes often revolve around Gas. Users might set too low a Gas limit, causing their transaction to fail and still pay the consumed Gas. Conversely, setting an excessively high Gas price can lead to overpaying for a transaction. Tools like Etherscan provide average Gas prices, and many wallets offer dynamic Gas price suggestions. Another common pitfall is misunderstanding transaction finality. While a transaction might be included in a block quickly, it's generally considered "final" only after a certain number of subsequent blocks have been added, reducing the chance of a chain reorganization. For critical operations, waiting for 6-12 block confirmations is a good safety practice. The security of smart contracts themselves is paramount; vulnerabilities like reentrancy attacks, integer overflows, and unchecked external calls have led to significant losses. Always ensure thorough auditing and testing of smart contract code before deployment.

screens.title: Ethereum and the EVM
screens.subtitle: How Ethereum runs smart contracts, consumes gas, and keeps a deterministic global state

narration.text: Welcome. In this short guided lesson you will understand why Ethereum is often described as a decentralized global computer, how it represents the network state with accounts, and why Gas is the economic control for computation. We will connect the idea of externally owned accounts and contract accounts to the lifecycle of a transaction, and end with how the Ethereum Virtual Machine deterministically executes bytecode on every node. You will see concrete examples: a human-controlled account sending a transaction to a deployed contract, a Gas calculation that determines transaction fees, and a simple storage contract life cycle from source code to stored value. Knowing these mechanics helps you reason about costs, avoid common mistakes like running out of Gas, and design smarter contracts that keep persistent storage minimal. By the end you will be able to describe the role of Gas in protecting the network, explain how the EVM isolates execution, and point to practical steps—testing, auditing, and waiting confirmations—to reduce risk. Keep these core ideas in mind as we move into objectives and step-by-step lessons that demonstrate compilation, deployment, and Gas accounting.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Ethereum is an account-based state machine where Gas enforces costs and the EVM provides an isolated, deterministic runtime for smart contract bytecode.

Ethereum and the EVM

Learn how Ethereum represents global state with accounts, uses Gas as computation fuel, and runs smart contract bytecode inside the Ethereum Virtual Machine. These ideas are the foundation for building, deploying, and securing smart contracts.

In this lesson
Account model, Gas mechanics, EVM execution, and a live deployment demo.

Account Model Snapshot

EOA

Contract Account
Holds code and storage. Executes only when it receives a transaction.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives guide our lesson sequence. First, you will explain Ethereum’s architecture: that it is an account-based state machine where transactions move the global state from one valid snapshot to the next. Second, you will differentiate Externally Owned Accounts and Contract Accounts, knowing that EOAs are controlled by private keys and initiate transactions while Contract Accounts run code when triggered. Third, you will describe Gas: its purpose as a metered unit of computation, how Gas limit and Gas price determine total fees, and why Gas prevents denial-of-service attacks. Finally, you will understand the Ethereum Virtual Machine as an isolated, stack-based runtime that executes compiled bytecode deterministically on every node. Each objective includes a practical takeaway: you will read simple transaction receipts, identify Gas used versus Gas limit, and recognize where persistent storage costs more than transient memory. These skills matter because they let you estimate costs, avoid common mistakes like underestimating Gas limits, and reason about contract security and finality. Verified competency milestones appear on each objective to help you track progress and practice with example scripts.

screens.title: Ethereum: a transaction-based state machine
screens.subtitle: How global state is represented and changed with each transaction

narration.text: Start with a clear definition. Ethereum operates as a transaction-based state machine: every valid transaction causes a transition from one global state to another. The global state includes account balances, contract code, and contract storage. This differs from UTXO models by using an account-centric approach, where addresses hold balances and code. For you as a developer or auditor, this model matters because it makes it straightforward to reason about persistent storage: a contract’s state variables are part of the global state and persist between transactions. A concrete example: when a user signs and sends a transaction that calls a contract's set function to store a number, the EVM executes the bytecode, updates the contract’s storage, and the global state reflects that new value. A common misconception is to treat transactions as isolated events; instead, each one mutates global state and subsequent transactions observe the updated values. Another point: determination and reproducibility are essential. The EVM runs the same bytecode on every node so all nodes reach the same resulting state. Why this matters practically: it enables trustless interactions and predictable contract behaviour, but it also means design choices that change storage like writing to state variables are permanent and cost Gas. Takeaway: think in terms of state transitions, not just single transactions, and design contracts with minimal costly state changes.

keyIdea.title: State machine insight
keyIdea.text: Each transaction transforms the shared global state; contracts store persistent data that future transactions will read and trust.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › State Machine
Ethereum as a state machine

Every transaction deterministically moves the global state. State holds accounts, code, and contract storage that persist between transactions.

Definition
A transaction-based state machine applies transactions to move the network from one valid global state to another.
Concrete example
An EOA calls a contract function to set a value. The EVM executes bytecode, updates storage, and the global state now includes the new value.
Common misconception
Transactions are not isolated; they change the shared state and affect later transactions. Treat state changes as persistent and costly.
Key Takeaway

Design contracts expecting persistent state changes; minimize unnecessary writes to keep Gas manageable and predictable.

Visual: Transaction flow
EOA
Contract Account
When the EOA sends a signed transaction, the network validates and the EVM executes code to update persistent storage. All nodes perform the same execution, ensuring deterministic state transitions.

screens.title: EOAs vs Contract Accounts
screens.subtitle: Who initiates actions and who reacts with code

narration.text: Let's compare Externally Owned Accounts and Contract Accounts in a way that clarifies who can do what. An EOA is controlled by a private key. Humans, scripts, or bots use EOAs to sign and send transactions, hold Ether, and initiate interactions. A Contract Account is controlled by deployed smart contract code. It has an address and storage, it can hold Ether, and it executes its code only when it receives a transaction from an EOA or another contract. A practical example: a user with an EOA calls a token contract's transfer function; the EOA pays Gas and triggers the contract code, which updates balances in persistent storage. A frequent mistake is to assume contracts can spontaneously run or be called without an external trigger; contract code runs only in response to a transaction. Also, both account types can hold Ether and both can interact with other contracts — the difference is control and initiation. For learners, remember: EOAs initiate, contract accounts react. This distinction guides security design—only an EOA can create the first invocation, so protect private keys and ensure contracts validate all incoming calls. Final question to reflect on: when you design a contract, which actions should be left to EOAs and which should the contract enforce internally?

keyIdea.title: Account difference
keyIdea.text: EOAs sign and initiate transactions; Contract Accounts contain code and execute only when invoked by transactions.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › EOA vs Contract
Externally Owned Account (EOA)

Controlled by a private key. Signs transactions and pays Gas to trigger activity on the network.

Characteristics
Holds Ether, signs transactions, initiates contract interactions.
Misconception
An EOA is not the same as a user interface; the EOA secures signing and private key custody matters for security.
Key Takeaway

Protect private keys and treat EOAs as the source of authority that must be secured.

Contract Account

Holds code and storage. Runs its code only when it receives a transaction from an EOA or another contract.

Characteristics
Has an address, stores persistent state, and can make internal calls to other contracts during execution.
Practical note
Design contracts to validate inputs and guard against patterns like unchecked external calls to avoid vulnerabilities.
Reflection
Decide which operations should be triggered only by EOAs and where contracts should enforce their own invariants.

screens.title: Gas: Ethereum's fuel
screens.subtitle: Why every operation costs Gas and how fees are computed

narration.text: Gas is the measure of computational effort on Ethereum. Every EVM operation, storage read or write, and log emission has a Gas cost. This mechanism serves two essential purposes: it prevents infinite loops and resource exhaustion by making computation cost money, and it economically incentivizes validators to include transactions by paying Gas fees. Users express how much they are willing to spend using two parameters: a Gas limit, which caps the maximum Gas the transaction can consume, and a Gas price, which sets the amount of Ether paid per Gas unit—commonly expressed in Gwei. The total transaction fee equals Gas used times Gas price. A concrete example is submitting a contract call that is estimated to use 50,000 Gas. If the Gas price is set at a given Gwei amount, the final fee equals that product. A common beginner mistake is setting the Gas limit too low; if execution hits the limit, the EVM reverts the state changes but the Gas spent until that point is still paid to the miner or validator. Another mistake is needlessly overpaying a very high Gas price for non-urgent transactions. Practical advice: use wallet suggestions or network explorers to choose a reasonable Gas price, and set the Gas limit slightly above the estimated use to avoid failed transactions. Consider Gas cost when designing contracts—avoid expensive persistent writes when a transient value suffices.

keyIdea.title: Gas formula
keyIdea.text: Transaction fee = Gas Used × Gas Price. Gas protects the network and pays validators for computation.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Gas Fundamentals
Gas explained

Gas quantifies computation and storage cost on Ethereum. It prevents runaway execution and compensates validators.

Gas parameters
Gas limit: maximum payable Gas. Gas price: Ether per Gas unit. Fee = Gas used × Gas price.
Why Gas matters
It prevents infinite loops and DoS attacks by making heavy computation costly, and it provides an economic incentive for validators.
Common mistakes
Setting gas limit too low causes reversion and still consumes Gas. Overpaying gas price wastes funds when the network is not congested.
Example: fee calculation
Estimated Gas used: 50,000
Gas price: user-selected (expressed in Gwei)
Total fee = Gas used × Gas price
Pro tip

Use wallet or explorer estimates and add a small buffer to the gas limit to prevent accidental reverts.

screens.title: What happens when a transaction runs out of Gas
screens.subtitle: Execution, reversion, and who pays for consumed Gas

narration.text: Understanding the out-of-Gas case is essential for safe development. When a transaction reaches the Gas limit during execution, the EVM stops further operations and reverts any state changes made by that transaction. Reversion means the contract's persistent state returns to its prior values as if the transaction never altered them. However, the Gas consumed up to the point of failure is not refunded—miners or validators keep it as compensation for the work done. A concrete example: you call a function that enters a loop due to unexpected input and consumes Gas until the Gas limit is reached. The function's state assignments are reverted, but you still pay the Gas used. A common beginner error is assuming a reverted transaction costs nothing; in reality, computational and storage fees until the failure are still paid. Another misconception is thinking reverts protect funds beyond Gas; reverts only undo state writes, not the Gas paid. Practical defenses include estimating Gas carefully, using limits slightly above estimates, adding input validation to avoid unintended loops, and testing on local networks to observe Gas consumption. Takeaway: always plan for Gas edge cases, perform local simulations, and validate inputs so transactions don't unexpectedly exhaust their Gas.

keyIdea.title: Reversion rule
keyIdea.text: If execution runs out of Gas the EVM reverts state changes but the Gas spent until failure is still charged.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Out-of-Gas Flow
Execution lifecycle when out of Gas
The EVM executes until Gas is exhausted, then reverts state changes but charges Gas for the work performed.
Step 1
Transaction executes, consuming Gas per EVM opcode.
Step 2
If Gas limit reached, the EVM halts and reverts state writes from that transaction.
Step 3
Gas consumed is still paid to the block proposer; revert does not refund spent Gas.
Concrete scenario
A loop runs due to unexpected input. If it exceeds the Gas limit the transaction reverts. The state is unchanged, but the sender loses the Gas paid while the loop executed.
Defensive checklist
  • Estimate Gas locally and add a small buffer to Gas limit.
  • Validate inputs to avoid unbounded loops or heavy computations.
  • Test on a local network to observe Gas consumption before mainnet deployment.

screens.title: The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM)
screens.subtitle: Stack-based, isolated, and deterministic execution of smart contract bytecode

narration.text: The Ethereum Virtual Machine is the runtime that executes smart contract bytecode on every node. It is stack-based and isolated: contracts cannot access the node’s file system or network resources, which protects node integrity and enforces determinism. When a developer writes Solidity, the compiler emits EVM bytecode that is deployed as a Contract Account. The EVM provides stack, memory, and persistent storage: the stack is used for short-lived computation, memory is transient for the duration of a call, and storage persists between transactions as part of the global state. A concrete example: a compiled function pushes operands onto the stack, computes a result in memory, and then writes a state variable to storage when committing. That final storage write is what contributes to long-term Gas cost. Misconceptions include thinking the EVM can directly access external data; it cannot, which is why oracles are needed to bridge off-chain data. Understanding the separation between stack, memory, and storage is critical for optimising Gas: storage writes are expensive, memory usage is cheaper but temporary. Takeaway: design contract logic to minimize storage writes and prefer transient memory when possible, verifying behaviour with local execution traces.

keyIdea.title: EVM roles
keyIdea.text: The EVM enforces deterministic execution across nodes and separates stack, memory, and storage for predictable cost and behaviour.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › EVM Architecture
What the EVM provides

A deterministic, isolated, stack-based virtual machine that executes compiled bytecode identically on every node.

Stack
Short-lived operand storage used during instruction execution.
Memory
Transient workspace during a call; cleared after execution completes.
Storage
Persistent contract state that contributes to global state and costs more Gas to modify.
Misconception
The EVM cannot access external systems directly; use oracles for off-chain data and expect increased complexity and Gas costs for such interactions.
Why separation matters
Storage writes are expensive and persist across transactions. Memory and stack are cheaper and ephemeral. Optimising where you place data will reduce transaction costs and improve contract performance.
Design hint
Cache transient values in memory during execution and write to storage only when you need persistent state changes.

screens.title: Solidity to bytecode: compilation and deployment
screens.subtitle: How source code becomes a Contract Account on the blockchain

narration.text: Compilation and deployment are the bridge from human-readable code to on-chain execution. When you write a contract in Solidity, a compiler translates it into EVM bytecode. That bytecode, along with an initial deployment transaction, is sent to the network. When the deployment transaction is mined, the bytecode is stored at the new contract address — that address becomes a Contract Account with code and empty or initial storage. A concrete example is our simple Storage contract: the Solidity source defines functions to set and get a value. The compiler produces bytecode; the deployer sends a transaction that includes the bytecode as payload. After mining, the contract address has code and persistent storage slots. A common misconception is to expect Solidity source to exist on-chain; the chain stores bytecode, not source files — source verification is an additional step services provide. For practical work: compile locally with Hardhat, inspect artifacts to see bytecode and ABI, then send the deployment transaction to a local or test network to observe the creation of the Contract Account. Takeaway: deployment transforms compile-time artifacts into an on-chain Contract Account that future EOAs and contracts will call.

keyIdea.title: Deployment insight
keyIdea.text: Deployment transaction stores compiled bytecode on-chain and creates a Contract Account that exposes callable functions.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Compile & Deploy
From source to contract

Compile Solidity to EVM bytecode using a tool like Hardhat. Deploy by sending the bytecode in a transaction; on mining the code is stored at an address.

Sample Solidity (Storage.sol)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract Storage {
  uint256 private storedData; // State variable to store a number

  event DataStored(uint256 newValue, address indexed sender);

  function set(uint256 x) public {
    storedData = x;
    emit DataStored(x, msg.sender);
  }

  function get() public view returns (uint256) {
    return storedData;
  }
}
Deployment script (illustrative)
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const Storage = await ethers.getContractFactory("Storage");
  const storage = await Storage.deploy();

  await storage.deployed();

  console.log("Storage contract deployed to:", storage.address);
}

main()
  .then(() => process.exit(0))
  .catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1); });
After deployment, the contract's bytecode is on-chain. The ABI remains off-chain but can be published to allow clients to call the contract functions.

screens.title: Storage vs Memory: gas and design trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Why persistent writes cost more and how to minimize them

narration.text: A practical optimization every developer must know is the difference between storage and memory cost. Contract storage writes modify the persistent state and are therefore expensive in Gas. Memory and the stack are temporary and cleared after execution, making them cheaper for intermediate calculations. Consider a function that computes a result and only needs to persist the final value: it is more Gas-efficient to keep intermediate values in memory and write a single storage update at the end. A concrete example: a function that aggregates several inputs then writes the result to a state variable — keeping aggregation in memory reduces the number of costly storage writes. Common misunderstandings include assuming memory persists across transactions or that storage writes are free. In reality, storage persists and contributes to global state size, so writes are not only costlier at runtime but also affect long-term chain state. Practical guidance: batch writes when possible, avoid unnecessary state variables, and use events or off-chain indexing for heavy read workloads rather than storing large arrays on-chain. Testing and profiling on a local network will reveal the Gas differences between strategies. Final takeaway: optimize for fewer persistent writes to reduce user costs and make your contracts more efficient.

keyIdea.title: Optimization insight
keyIdea.text: Prefer transient memory and stack for intermediate work; minimize storage writes to reduce Gas and long-term state growth.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Storage vs Memory
Storage vs Memory

Storage is persistent and expensive. Memory and stack are transient and cheaper. Use this to design cost-efficient functions.

When to write storage
Write to storage only for values that must persist across transactions. Use memory for temporary computation.
Concrete pattern
Aggregate or compute in memory, then perform a single storage write for the final result to minimize cost.
Design advice

Avoid large on-chain arrays for archives; prefer events and off-chain indexing for heavy read workloads to save Gas and state size.

Check your understanding
  • Why is a single storage write cheaper than multiple writes? (Answer: fewer persistent modifications reduce Gas.)
  • When is storing data on-chain justified? (Answer: when persistence and on-chain verification are required.)
  • What is a common off-chain pattern to avoid storage costs? (Answer: emit events and index data off-chain.)

screens.title: Deploying the Storage contract with Hardhat
screens.subtitle: Local deployment, interaction, and observing gas used

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough connects the theory to the terminal workflow you will run locally. First, set up a Hardhat project and place the Storage. sol file into the contracts directory. Compile with the Hardhat compiler to produce artifacts that include bytecode and ABI. Next, start a local node and run a deployment script that deploys the contract and calls its set function. You will observe terminal output showing the contract address, the initial stored value, the transaction hash for the set call, and the new stored value. Importantly, the output will also show Gas used for the transaction; this is where you see Gas accounting in practice. A concrete example is setting the value 42 in the Storage contract: the deployment script logs the address, reads the initial value of zero, sends a transaction to set 42, waits for mining with tx. wait(), and then reads back the updated value. A common beginner mistake is not waiting for tx. wait() and assuming the value has changed immediately; in reality you must wait for the transaction to be mined to observe state changes. Final takeaway: run these steps on a local network to safely inspect receipts, Gas used, and the contract’s state lifecycle before deploying to public testnets or mainnet.

keyIdea.title: Lab insight
keyIdea.text: Deploy locally, call functions, and use transaction receipts to inspect Gas used and confirm state changes after mining.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Deployment Demo
Deployment script
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const Storage = await ethers.getContractFactory("Storage");
  const storage = await Storage.deploy();

  await storage.deployed();

  console.log("Storage contract deployed to:", storage.address);

  console.log("Current stored data:", (await storage.get()).toString());

  const setValue = 42;
  const tx = await storage.set(setValue);
  await tx.wait(); // Wait for the transaction to be mined

  console.log(`Set stored data to ${setValue}. Transaction hash: ${tx.hash}`);
  console.log("New stored data:", (await storage.get()).toString());
}

main()
  .then(() => process.exit(0))
  .catch((error) => { console.error(error); process.exit(1); });
Sample terminal output (local node)
Storage contract deployed to: 0xAB...123
Current stored data: 0
Set stored data to 42. Transaction hash: 0xTX...789
New stored data: 42
Note: transaction receipts include Gas used; watch for the Gas used number to appear after tx.wait()
Common mistake
Not awaiting tx.wait() and reading contract state before the transaction is mined. Always wait for mining to confirm state changes.

screens.title: Transaction finality and common security pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Confirmations, reorg risk, and contract vulnerabilities

narration.text: Two important practical topics are transaction finality and contract security. Transaction finality on Ethereum is probabilistic: inclusion in a block makes a transaction visible, but a chain reorganization can replace blocks. For critical operations, waiting for multiple block confirmations—commonly suggested between six and twelve—reduces the chance of reorgs reversing your transaction. A concrete example: a high-value transfer may be broadcast and included quickly, but waiting several confirmations gives higher assurance that the block will persist. Regarding security, common vulnerabilities include reentrancy, unchecked external calls, and integer overflows. These issues can lead to significant losses if contracts are not thoroughly audited. A frequent beginner error is trusting that a successful transaction receipt automatically means the contract is secure; it only signals that the state changed as intended, not that the code is safe. Practical steps: rely on code audits, unit tests, and local simulations; use patterns that minimize external call surface and validate every external input. Takeaway: combine confirmation discipline for transaction finality with rigorous security practices to reduce operational and financial risk when deploying and interacting with contracts. Transaction finality and common security pitfalls means wait for confirmations to reduce reorg risk and prioritize security audits to avoid vulnerabilities like reentrancy or unchecked calls.. In practical terms, confirmations, reorg risk, and contract vulnerabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Finality & security
keyIdea.text: Wait for confirmations to reduce reorg risk and prioritize security audits to avoid vulnerabilities like reentrancy or unchecked calls.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Finality & Security
Transaction finality

A transaction is included in a block quickly, but confirmations reduce the risk of a chain reorganisation reversing it. For critical operations wait multiple confirmations.

Practical rule
Wait 6–12 confirmations for high-value or irreversible operations to lower reorg risk.
Why it matters

Confirmations trade speed for assurance; plan your application UX to account for waiting where finality matters.

Common security pitfalls
Reentrancy, unchecked external calls, and arithmetic issues are recurring causes of exploits. Auditing and testing are essential defenses.
Example vulnerability
A contract that transfers Ether before updating internal balances can allow reentrancy attacks. Always update state before external calls when appropriate.
Checklist
  • Write unit tests and integration tests.
  • Run local simulations to estimate Gas and detect reverts.
  • Get independent audits before mainnet deployment.
Reflection
Does your contract require immediate finality? If so, bake in confirmation waits and stronger checks around external interactions.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's close with three compact concepts to remember. First, Ethereum is an account-based, transaction-driven state machine: transactions move the global state and contract storage persists across them. Second, Gas is the fuel and economic control for computation: set Gas limit and Gas price sensibly because total fees equal Gas used times Gas price, and running out of Gas reverts state while still charging for consumed computation. Third, the EVM executes compiled bytecode deterministically and in isolation: separate stack, memory, and storage inform cost and behaviour, and contracts cannot access external data without oracles. Keep these three concepts handy when designing, testing, and deploying contracts. As a short practice, run the provided Storage contract on a local network, inspect the transaction receipts for Gas used, and confirm storage changes only after the transaction is mined. That practice ties the theory directly to working code and safe deployment habits.

keyIdea.title: Three essentials
keyIdea.text: State machine, Gas accounting, and the EVM's deterministic runtime are the foundation for secure and efficient smart contracts.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Key Concepts
Ethereum
A decentralized, account-based platform where transactions change a shared global state.
Gas
A unit of computation cost. Fee = Gas used × Gas price; prevents infinite loops and compensates validators.
EVM
The isolated, deterministic runtime that executes compiled bytecode and enforces stack, memory, and storage separation.
Summary takeaway
Design with Gas in mind, test locally, wait confirmations for critical operations, and audit contracts to reduce security risk.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact memory aids for practical use

narration.text: Keep three quick reference cards in your mental toolkit. First, remember the distinction: EOAs initiate and Contract Accounts execute when triggered. Second, Gas is the economic throttle: always check Gas estimates, set a reasonable limit, and expect that consumed Gas is paid even on revert. Third, the EVM enforces determinism and isolation: storage changes persist across transactions and are expensive, while memory and stack are temporary and cheaper. Use these memory aids when you're designing, testing, or preparing a deployment script. They will help you make cost-efficient and safer choices, and will guide your testing checklist before moving code to a public network. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means initiator vs reactor, gas as throttle, and evm separation—use these to guide design and deployment choices.. In practical terms, three compact memory aids for practical use. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.1 › Quick Reference
Initiator vs Reactor
EOAs sign and start transactions; contracts run only when invoked.
Gas Mindset
Estimate Gas, set an appropriate limit, and expect to pay for consumed Gas even on revert.
EVM Separation
Stack and memory are ephemeral; storage is persistent and expensive. Plan writes accordingly.
Final quick tip
Test and audit locally, inspect Gas used in receipts, and wait confirmations for important transactions.
